nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.body_markdown: Natural numbers are those numbers that we use for counting. The set of whole numbers includes all the natural numbers along with zero. In this chapter, we will begin by revising whole numbers and the ways of grouping and classifying them. We will also be working with different properties of operations with numbers. To see how whole numbers are used in real life, we will solve some word problems involving these numbers.

nodes.title: Ordering and comparing whole numbers
nodes.subject: maths
nodes.body_markdown: When writing whole numbers, you should pay careful attention to the place value of each digit in the number. This is especially important when you do calculations with whole numbers, because placing the digits incorrectly will cause errors. A number that cannot be expressed as a product of two whole numbers, except as the product of 1 multiplied by the number itself, is called a prime number . For example, the number 4 can be expressed as 4 × 1 or 2 × 2. And the number 12 can be expressed as 12 × 1 or 6 × 2 or 4 × 3. Follow these rules to decide if each number is even, odd, or neither: Consecutive means “next to each other” or “following each other without missing anything”. Sometimes, another property of numbers is used to clarify which consecutive numbers should be used. For example, if we need to decide whether a list of given numbers shows consecutive odd numbers or not, then we need to use the properties of odd numbers. Similarly, the list of even numbers will start at 2 and count up in twos. We use a place value table to compare whole numbers. This is especially useful when working with big numbers. Place value tables let us look closely at what the digits in numbers mean. Digits in places further left represent bigger numbers.
